title: Reading hadith today
hook: reading hadith with its context and a teacher

segments.voice: Yesterday, sharh, and your line: explained for us. Did you read past a puzzling line before deciding what it meant? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. Stop the sentence there and it sounds like a call to back your own side no matter what. The people who first heard it seem to have stumbled too, because in Sahih al-Bukhari someone asks the Prophet ﷺ: helping him when he's wronged, that we understand, but how do we help him when he's the oppressor? And the answer turns the whole thing around. By stopping him from oppressing. Half a hadith, heard alone, pointed the opposite way from the whole. Today: reading hadith today.
screen: `HELP YOUR BROTHER.` → `HOW, IF HE'S THE OPPRESSOR?` → `BY STOPPING HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the whole text. Reports travel now as screenshots and captions, trimmed to fit. A basic habit of hadith study is the one you just heard: find the full report, with its question and its answer, before deciding what it says. Second, the setting. Scholars paid attention to the occasion of a saying, sabab al-wurud: who asked, what had just happened, who was being spoken to. When Abdullah ibn Amr was told that his body had a right over him, it was because he had been fasting every day and standing in prayer every night. Lift that line out of its story and it can be made to say almost anything. Third, the neighbors. A single report sits among others on the same subject, and among the verses of the Qur'an. Jurists read them side by side, and the schools of law sometimes reached different conclusions from the same texts. That's where this year turns next. Fourth, the person. In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a saying of the early scholar Muhammad ibn Sirin: this knowledge is religion, so look carefully at whom you take your religion from. The chain didn't stop when the books were finished. Students went on reading the collections aloud in front of teachers, who could say: this word means this, that report explains this one, and here the scholars differ. That is still how this tradition reads hadith at its most careful. The words, the setting, the other texts, and someone who has walked the road before you.
screen: `FIND THE WHOLE REPORT.` · `SABAB AL-WURUD: THE SETTING.` · `READ IT BESIDE ITS NEIGHBORS.` · `LOOK AT WHOM YOU LEARN FROM.`

segments.voice: The practice: ask someone about a hadith. First, find the one to ask about. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a hadith you've heard quoted, maybe recently, maybe on a screen. Say it to yourself as you heard it. Now put today's questions to it, gently. Is that the whole of it? Who was being spoken to? What else is said on this? Don't answer them. Just notice which ones you can't. Then think of one person you could ask: an imam, a teacher, a friend who studies. Hold their face in mind for a breath. The bell holds the time.
Reading hadith today. Taking a report whole, in its setting, beside the other texts, and with someone who has studied it. Today's word.
Your line: with a teacher. Today, take the hadith you thought of to one person who has studied it, and ask what they understand by it. Tomorrow: hadith close. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims who study hadith read the collections with a teacher, in a class or circle, who explains each report's setting, its other versions, and how scholars have understood it.

fork.setup: a friend sends you half a hadith that seems to back your side in an argument. what do you do?
options: send it on and win the argument.
find the full report and ask someone who knows it.
decide hadith are too confusing to read at all.
fork.reveal: the first hearers did just that with "help your brother": they asked, and the answer turned the half they'd heard around.

notes: Bukhari 2444 (Anas: help your brother, oppressor or oppressed; 'by stopping him'): confirm number (also 2443, 6952).

Abdullah ibn Amr callback (day 1113, Bukhari 1975): 'your body has a right over you' tied to his vow to fast daily; confirm.
'Students went on reading the collections aloud in front of teachers' and 'teachers in this tradition say' are general descriptions with no dates; confirm the framing.
